home.pilotText: This is the pilot version: complete chapters with their interactive charts, Python code that runs in your browser and self-checking exercises, plus the glossary and the formula summary. More material will arrive in stages.
home.how1: Each chapter starts with the idea and a worked example; the more rigorous «Going further» section at the end unfolds if you want it.
home.how2: The charts are driven by sliders, also from the keyboard; each one tells you what to look for.
home.how3: The Python code runs in your browser: nothing to install and no data sent to any server.

tC.title: From the binomial tree to Black-Scholes
tC.chartDesc: Price of a European call and put with the Black and Scholes (1973) formula, and price of the call with a binomial tree of 1 to N steps. Move the controls to see how they change.
tC.observe: The call is always worth more than it would pay if it expired today: that difference is the time value, and it grows with volatility and maturity. The European put, by contrast, can be worth less than its payoff when it is deep in the money, because receiving K at expiry is worth less than receiving it today. In the binomial tree panel, the price oscillates around the exact one and approaches it as steps are added.
tC.heading: Interactive chart
tC.noTree: with so few steps the tree is not valid
tC.descLeft: With the stock at {S} and strike {K}, the call is worth {c} and the put {p}. The dashed lines are what they pay at expiry.
tC.descRight: With {n} steps the tree gives {t} for the call; Black-Scholes gives {c}.

tA.title: The best of N strategies with no skill
tA.chartDesc: Simulates N strategies whose true Sharpe ratio is zero and measures each one's Sharpe with a few years of data. Move the number of strategies and the years of data.
tA.observe: Even though no strategy has any skill, the best of many looks excellent: its Sharpe grows roughly like √(2 ln N) times the standard error. More years of data reduce the error, but do not make the effect go away.

tA.descRight: With {N} strategies, the expected maximum Sharpe is {e}; in this simulation it was {b}.
tA.statSe: Standard error of the Sharpe with {Y} years

tA.describe: {N} strategies with no skill are tested with {Y} years of data. The standard error of the Sharpe is {se}, and the best scores a Sharpe of {b} by pure chance (on average {e} would be expected).
tA.tableCaption: Expected maximum Sharpe of N strategies with no skill and {Y} years of data
tB.title: What costs eat up
tB.chartDesc: Sharpe ratio of a strategy before and after costs by how much it trades per year, and the market impact of an order by its size (square-root law).
tB.observe: Every time the portfolio trades, you pay: the net Sharpe falls in a straight line with turnover and reaches zero when the annual cost equals the return. Impact grows with the square root of the order size: doubling the order does not double the impact, but it is not free either.

tB.descRight: An order of {q} of daily volume, with daily volatility of {s}, moves the price by about {i}.
tB.statBe: Turnover that leaves the Sharpe at 0
tB.describe: Trading {t} times a year at a cost of {c} per trade loses {a} a year, and the Sharpe goes from {g} to {n}. An order of {q} of daily volume with daily volatility of {s} moves the price by about {i}.
tB.tableCaption: Annual cost and net Sharpe by turnover (cost per trade: {c})
tD.title: A spread that reverts to its mean
tD.chartDesc: Simulates the spread between two cointegrated prices, sₜ = φ·sₜ₋₁ + εₜ, and shows its reversion half-life. With φ = 1 the spread is a random walk.
tD.observe: With φ below 1 the spread wanders off but comes back to zero again and again, within a stable band. The closer φ is to 1, the longer the half-life and the slower the return; with φ = 1 the band disappears and the spread no longer comes back.
tD.heading: Interactive chart
tD.descLeft: Spread with φ = {p} over {n} days; it crosses zero {c} times.
tD.descRight: With φ = {p}, the half-life is {h} days.
tD.rwNote: (random walk: it does not come back)
tD.describe: With φ = {p}, the spread has a half-life of {h} days and crosses zero {c} times in {n} days.
tD.describeRw: With φ = {p}, the spread is a random walk: it has no half-life and does not reliably return to zero (in {n} days it crosses it {c} times).
tD.tableCaption: Half-life and stationary standard deviation by φ (noise with standard deviation 1)
tE.title: The drawdown curve
tE.chartDesc: Simulates the value of a portfolio over some years and plots how far below its previous peak it is at each moment. Change the volatility, the years or the seed.
tE.observe: The maximum drawdown almost always gets worse with more volatility and with more years of sample, even if the strategy is the same. Notice also how long the portfolio spends below its peak: recovering from a 50% drawdown requires a 100% gain.
